facts.quote: A market order is an order to buy or sell a stock at the best available price.  Generally, a market order will be executed immediately.
facts.claim: A market order buys or sells at the best price available and generally fills right away.

facts.quote: However, the price at which a market order will be executed is not guaranteed.
facts.claim: A market order's price is not guaranteed.

facts.quote: parts of a large market order may execute at different prices due to lack of liquidity at a price at the time of execution.
facts.claim: One large order can fill in parts, at several prices, when one price lacks enough shares.

facts.quote: A limit order is an order to buy or sell a stock at a specific price or better.
facts.claim: A limit order trades only at your price or better.

facts.quote: A buy limit order can only be executed at the limit price or lower, and a sell limit order can only be executed at the limit price or higher.
facts.claim: A buy limit fills at the limit or lower; a sell limit fills at the limit or higher.

facts.quote: A limit order is not guaranteed to execute.  A limit order can only be filled if the stock’s market price reaches the limit price.
facts.claim: A limit order may never fill.

facts.quote: A stop order, also referred to as a stop-loss order, is an order to buy or sell a stock once the price of the stock reaches a specified price, known as the stop price.
facts.claim: A stop order, also called a stop-loss order, acts once price reaches the stop price.

facts.quote: When the stop price is reached, a stop order becomes a market order.
facts.claim: At the stop price, a stop order turns into a market order.

facts.quote: buy stop order is entered at a stop price above the current market price. Investors generally use a buy stop order to limit a loss or to protect a profit on a stock that they have sold short.
facts.claim: A buy stop sits above the current price; investors generally use it to limit a loss or protect a profit on a short.

facts.quote: sell stop order is entered at a stop price below the current market price. Investors generally use a sell stop order to limit a loss or to protect a profit on a stock that they own.
facts.claim: A sell stop sits below the current price; it limits a loss or protects a profit on shares you own.

facts.quote: The stop price is not the guaranteed execution price for a stop order.  The stop price is a trigger that causes the stop order to become a market order.
facts.claim: The stop price is a trigger, not a promised fill price.

facts.quote: Investors should carefully select the stop price they use for a stop order since short-term market fluctuations in a stock’s price can activate a stop order.
facts.claim: Short-term swings can set off a stop, so choose the stop price with care.

facts.quote: Once the stop price is reached, a stop-limit order becomes a limit order that will be executed at a specified price (or better).
facts.claim: At the stop price, a stop-limit turns into a limit order.

facts.quote: As with all limit orders, a stop-limit order may not be executed if the stock’s price moves away from the specified limit price.
facts.claim: A stop-limit may not fill if price moves past its limit.

facts.quote: The stop price and the limit price for a stop-limit order do not have to be the same price.
facts.claim: A stop-limit's stop price and limit price can be different.

facts.quote: A trailing stop order is a stop or stop limit order in which the stop price is not a specific price.
facts.claim: A trailing stop's stop price is not a fixed number.

facts.quote: Instead, the stop price is either a defined percentage or dollar amount, above or below the current market price of the security
facts.claim: The trail is a set percent or dollar amount away from the market price.

facts.quote: As the price of the security moves in a favorable direction the trailing stop price adjusts or “trails” the market price of the security by the specified amount.
facts.claim: When price moves your way, the trailing stop follows it by the set amount.

facts.quote: However, if the security’s price moves in an unfavorable direction the trailing stop price remains fixed, and the order will be triggered if the security’s price reaches the trailing stop price.
facts.claim: When price moves against you, the trailing stop stays put and triggers if price reaches it.

facts.quote: The price of XYZ peaks at $24 then starts to drop (not in your favor).  Your trailing stop price will remain at $23.
facts.claim: In the SEC's example, a $1 trail under a $24 peak holds at $23 on the drop.

facts.quote: Investors should carefully select the trailing stop price they use for a trailing stop order since short-term market fluctuations in a stock’s price can activate a trailing stop order.
facts.claim: Short-term swings can set off a trailing stop.

facts.quote: Unless an investor specifies a time frame for the expiration of an order, orders to buy and sell a stock are “Day” orders, meaning they are good only during the trading day that the order is entered.
facts.claim: Unless you pick a time frame, an order is a Day order, good only for the day you enter it.

facts.quote: Day orders, if not executed, generally cancel at the end of regular trading hours of the trading day that they are entered and will not carry over to the extended hours session or the next trading day.
facts.claim: An unfilled Day order cancels at the close and does not carry into after-hours or the next day.

facts.quote: A GTC order is an order to buy or sell a stock that lasts until it is executed in full or it is canceled.
facts.claim: A GTC order lasts until it fills in full or is canceled.

facts.quote: the time limit that an investor can leave a GTC order open may vary based on the brokerage firm.
facts.claim: How long a GTC order can stay open varies by broker.

facts.quote: An IOC order is an order to buy or sell a stock that must be executed immediately.  Any portion of the order that cannot be filled immediately will be canceled.
facts.claim: IOC: fill what can fill right away and cancel the rest.

facts.quote: An FOK order is an order to buy or sell a stock that must be executed immediately in its entirety; otherwise, the entire order will be canceled
facts.claim: FOK: the whole order fills right away, or the whole order cancels.

facts.quote: (i.e., no partial execution of the order is allowed)
facts.claim: A fill-or-kill order never takes a partial fill.

facts.quote: An AON order is an order to buy or sell a stock that must be executed in its entirety, or not executed at all.
facts.claim: AON: the whole order or nothing.

facts.quote: However, unlike the FOK order, an AON order that is not executed immediately will remain active until it is executed or it is canceled.
facts.claim: Unlike FOK, an AON order that can't fill right away stays active.

facts.quote: A market or limit order that must be executed at the closing price. Any balance not executed as part of the closing trade is canceled.
facts.claim: An on-close order fills at the closing price; any part that misses the closing trade cancels.

facts.quote: A stop order may be triggered by a short-term, intraday price move that results in an execution price for the stop order that is substantially worse than the stock’s closing price for the day.
facts.claim: A quick intraday move can set off a stop and fill it far worse than the day's close.

facts.quote: The execution price an investor receives for this market order can deviate significantly from the stop price due to the prices of available liquidity when the market order executes.
facts.claim: A triggered stop can fill far from the stop price.

facts.quote: Unless you specify otherwise, your broker will enter your order as a market order.
facts.claim: If you don't say otherwise, your broker enters a market order.

facts.quote: “Price improvement” is the opportunity, but not the guarantee, for an order to be executed at a better price than the current quote.
facts.claim: A fill can come in better than the quote, but that is never promised.

walkthroughs.title: Market, limit, stop
steps: A market order says: fill me now at the best price available. The fill is close to sure. The price isn't.
A limit order says: my price or better. You control the price, but it may never fill.
A stop order waits. When price reaches the stop price, it becomes a market order.
A stop-limit becomes a limit order instead. Your price is protected, but the fill isn't.

walkthroughs.title: How long it lives, how much fills
steps: Every order has a time in force. Pick nothing and it's usually a day order.
A day order that doesn't fill generally cancels at the close. It won't carry into after-hours or tomorrow.
Good 'til canceled stays live until it fills or you cancel, within your broker's time limit.
IOC takes what fills now and cancels the rest. FOK is all of it now, or nothing.

walkthroughs.title: Short words
steps: A short sale sells shares you don't own. Your broker usually lends them to you, and the loan can carry a fee.
Before the short, the broker needs a locate: good reason to believe the shares can be borrowed.
To close a short you buy the shares back. That's covering, entered as buy to cover.
When many shorts cover at once, their buying pushes price higher. That's a short squeeze.

questions.q: What does a market order tell your broker?
choices: Trade now at the best price available
Trade only at my limit price or better
Trade once the price hits my trigger
Trade at the day's closing price
questions.answer: Trade now at the best price available
questions.why: Trade now at the best price available. It generally fills right away, but the price you get isn't guaranteed.
questions.lesson_line: A market order buys you a fill, not a price.

wrong.Trade only at my limit price or better: That's a limit order. It protects your price and may never fill.
wrong.Trade once the price hits my trigger: That's a stop order. It waits for the stop price, then becomes a market order.
wrong.Trade at the day's closing price: That's an on-close order, a separate instruction you have to choose.

questions.q: Unless you choose otherwise, brokers typically enter an order as a market order.
questions.why: True. FINRA and the SEC both say the default is a market order unless you specify otherwise. Check what your own ticket is set to.
questions.lesson_line: Read the order type before you send. A market order sets no price limit.

questions.q: Tap the word that fits the blank.
questions.sentence: I'll pay $25.40 and not a cent more, so I'm using a ___ order.
questions.why: Limit. A buy limit can only fill at your limit price or lower, so $25.40 is the most you'll pay.
questions.lesson_line: Name your price with a limit. The trade-off is that it may never fill.

questions.q: A sell limit order at $30.00 can fill at $29.90.
questions.why: False. A sell limit only fills at your limit price or higher. $29.90 is below it.
questions.lesson_line: Buy limit: your price or lower. Sell limit: your price or higher.

questions.q: On a limit order, what is the limit price?
choices: The worst price you'll accept
The price that triggers the order
The price you're sure to get
The last trade before you sent it
questions.why: The worst price you'll accept. If the order fills, you get your limit price or better, never worse.
questions.lesson_line: The limit is your line in the sand. Better can happen. Worse can't.

wrong.The price that triggers the order: That's the stop price on a stop or stop-limit order.
wrong.The price you're sure to get: Nothing is sure. A limit order may not fill at all, and it can fill better.
wrong.The last trade before you sent it: That's the last price. It sets nothing on your order.

questions.q: What kind of limit order is that?
questions.story: The quote is $10.00 bid, $10.05 ask. You send a buy limit order at $10.10.
choices: Marketable: it can fill right away
Non-marketable: it waits for a seller
A stop-limit waiting on a trigger
questions.answer: Marketable: it can fill right away
questions.why: Marketable. Your buy limit is at or above the best ask, so it can trade right away, and never above $10.10.
questions.lesson_line: A buy limit at or above the ask is marketable. It acts fast and still caps your price.

wrong.Non-marketable: it waits for a seller: That would be a buy limit below the ask, at the bid for example. Yours already reaches the sellers.
wrong.A stop-limit waiting on a trigger: There's no stop price here. It's a plain limit order, live as soon as you send it.

questions.q: What does a stop order do?
choices: Becomes a market order at a trigger
Fills only at your price or better
Cancels unless it is filled right away
Sells at exactly the stop price shown
questions.answer: Becomes a market order at a trigger
questions.why: Becomes a market order at a set price. When the stop price is reached, the stop turns into a market order.
questions.lesson_line: A stop is a trigger. Once it fires, you get the market.

wrong.Sells at exactly the stop price shown: The stop price is a trigger, not a promised fill. The fill can come in worse.

questions.q: Tap the word that fits the blank.
questions.sentence: Another name for a stop order is a ___ order.
questions.why: Stop-loss. The SEC says a stop order is also called a stop-loss order. Same order, two names.
questions.lesson_line: Stop and stop-loss name the same order.

questions.q: On a stop order, what is the stop price?
choices: The price that sets the order off
The price your shares will sell at
The worst price you'll accept
Your average cost on the trade
questions.answer: The price that sets the order off
questions.why: The price that sets the order off. FINRA calls it the trigger price. Once it's reached, the order goes to market.
questions.lesson_line: Stop price means trigger. It is not the price you get.

wrong.The price your shares will sell at: Not promised. The stop turns into a market order, and the fill can be worse.
wrong.The worst price you'll accept: That's a limit price. A plain stop has no limit.
wrong.Your average cost on the trade: That's your cost. A stop price sits wherever you choose to put it.

questions.q: A stop-loss order ends your loss right at the stop price.
questions.why: False. A stop-loss is a stop order. At the stop price it becomes a market order. In a fast market or a gap, the fill can be far worse.
questions.lesson_line: The name sounds like a promise. It's a trigger, and gaps and fast markets go right through it.

questions.q: Which order sits above the current price and buys at market once price rises to it?
choices: Buy stop
Buy limit
Sell stop
Sell limit
questions.why: Buy stop. It's entered above the current price, and when price reaches it, it becomes a market order to buy.
questions.lesson_line: Buy stops sit above the price. Use them to buy strength or to protect a short.

wrong.Buy limit: A buy limit fills at your price or lower. Placed above the price, it can fill right away instead of waiting.
wrong.Sell stop: A sell stop sits below the price, to sell shares you own.
wrong.Sell limit: A sell limit above the price sells into strength. It doesn't buy.

questions.q: Which order does that?
questions.story: You sold a stock short at $30. You want out automatically if it rises to $32.
choices: A buy stop at $32
A sell stop at $32
A buy limit at $32
questions.why: A buy stop at $32. It sits above the price and turns into a market buy if the stock rises to it, closing the short.
questions.lesson_line: Short a stock and your stop is a buy stop above. Set it when you enter.

wrong.A sell stop at $32: A sell stop sells. You're short, so getting out means buying.
wrong.A buy limit at $32: A buy limit at $32 sits above the price, so it can buy right away instead of waiting for $32.

questions.q: What happened to your shares?
questions.story: Your sell stop sits at $45. At 10 a.m. the stock trades down to $44.80 for a few minutes, then rallies. It closes at $47.
choices: The stop sold them on the dip
Nothing, stops only count at the close
They sold at the $47 close
questions.answer: The stop sold them on the dip
questions.why: The stop sold them on the dip. A short intraday move can set off a stop, even when the stock closes well above it.
questions.lesson_line: A stop doesn't wait for the close. Put it where the trade is wrong, not inside normal noise.

wrong.Nothing, stops only count at the close: A stop triggers when price reaches it during the day. It doesn't wait for the close.
wrong.They sold at the $47 close: Once the dip set it off, the stop became a market order and sold then, not at the close.

questions.q: What is a stop-limit order?
choices: A stop that becomes a limit order
A limit order with no time limit
A stop that follows the price up
A stop that fills all or none of it
questions.answer: A stop that becomes a limit order
questions.why: A stop that becomes a limit order. Once the stop price is reached, it can only fill at your limit price or better.
questions.lesson_line: Stop-limit: the stop says when, the limit says how bad a price you'll take.

wrong.A limit order with no time limit: That's a limit order marked good 'til canceled (GTC).
wrong.A stop that fills all or none of it: All-or-none is a size condition, not a stop-limit.

questions.q: Which order says exactly that?
questions.story: You own 300 shares, trading at $42. You want out if it falls to $40, but you won't sell below $39.50, even if that means no sale.
choices: Sell stop-limit: stop $40, limit $39.50
Sell a plain stop at $40, no limit
Sell limit at $39.50, as a day order
Sell trailing stop with a $0.50 trail
questions.why: Sell stop-limit, stop $40, limit $39.50. At $40 it becomes a limit order, and it can only sell at $39.50 or better.
questions.lesson_line: A stop-limit protects your price. The cost is that it may not sell at all.

wrong.Sell a plain stop at $40, no limit: A plain stop becomes a market order at $40 and can sell below $39.50 in a fast drop.
wrong.Sell limit at $39.50, as a day order: That's below the price, so it can sell right away. It doesn't wait for $40.
wrong.Sell trailing stop with a $0.50 trail: That stop follows price up and sits only $0.50 under it. It isn't the $40 trigger you asked for.

questions.q: In a fast drop straight through both prices, a sell stop-limit can leave you still holding the stock.
questions.why: True. Once triggered it's a limit order. If price falls past your limit before it fills, it just sits there unfilled.
questions.lesson_line: If getting out matters most, a stop-limit can fail you. Know which you need before the drop.

questions.q: What is a trailing stop?
choices: A stop that follows price by a gap
A stop parked at your entry price
A stop that only counts at the close
A stop that turns into a limit order
questions.answer: A stop that follows price by a gap
questions.why: A stop that follows price by a set gap. The gap is a percent or a dollar amount. It moves when price moves your way and holds still when it doesn't.
questions.lesson_line: A trailing stop moves one way only: in your favor.

wrong.A stop parked at your entry price: A stop at your entry is a fixed level. A trailing stop keeps adjusting.
wrong.A stop that only counts at the close: Stops trigger when price reaches them during the day.
wrong.A stop that turns into a limit order: That's a stop-limit. A plain trailing stop becomes a market order. What makes it trailing is that its stop price follows the market.

questions.q: You buy at $30 and set a sell trailing stop $2 below the price. It climbs to $37.40, then dips to $36. Where is your stop now?
questions.why: $35.40. The stop trails the high by $2: $37.40 less $2. On the dip to $36 it holds at $35.40.
questions.lesson_line: A trailing stop tracks the high, not your entry.

questions.q: When the stock drops, a sell trailing stop moves down with it.
questions.why: False. It only moves when price moves your way. On a drop it stays fixed, and it triggers if price reaches it.
questions.lesson_line: Up, it follows. Down, it waits for you at the line.

questions.q: What's the likely problem?
questions.story: You set a sell trailing stop $0.25 below the price. The stock normally swings about $2 in a day. Your plan is to hold for weeks.
choices: Normal swings will stop you out
It will never trigger on a drop
It turns into a limit order
It moves down on red days
questions.answer: Normal swings will stop you out
questions.why: Normal swings will stop you out. Short-term moves can set off a trailing stop, and a trail that tight sits inside the stock's ordinary daily range.
questions.lesson_line: Set the trail wider than the stock's normal noise, or noise will take you out.

wrong.It will never trigger on a drop: It triggers when price falls to it. With a trail that tight, that's almost any dip.
wrong.It turns into a limit order: A plain trailing stop becomes a market order when it triggers.
wrong.It moves down on red days: It never moves down. On a drop it holds still.

questions.q: Where does your buy stop trigger?
questions.story: You're short at $40 with a $3 trailing buy stop. The stock falls to a low of $31, then bounces.
choices: At $34
At $43
At $37
questions.why: At $34. A trailing buy stop follows the lowest price down, $3 above it. From the $31 low, that's $34.
questions.lesson_line: On a short the trail follows the lows. Every new low pulls your stop down.

wrong.At $43: That's $3 above your entry, where it started. It moved down as the stock fell.
wrong.At $37: That's your entry minus the trail. On a short the stop sits above the price, and it trails the low.

questions.q: What is a bracket order?
choices: An entry with linked stop and target
Two orders where one cancels the other
A stop that follows the price up
An order to buy within a price range
questions.answer: An entry with linked stop and target
questions.why: An entry with a stop and target attached. When the entry fills, a take-profit and a stop go in, linked so one filling cancels the other.
questions.lesson_line: A bracket puts the whole plan on the ticket: entry, stop, target.

wrong.Two orders where one cancels the other: That's an OCO. A bracket uses an OCO for its exits, but it starts with the entry.
wrong.An order to buy within a price range: The name sounds like a range, but it isn't one. A bracket is one entry plus a linked stop and target.

questions.q: What kind of order did you send?
questions.story: You send one ticket: buy 200 shares at $25.40. When it fills, a sell limit at $28.00 and a sell stop at $24.20 go in, linked.
choices: Bracket order
Trailing stop
Stop-limit order
Fill-or-kill
questions.why: Bracket order. The entry fills first, then a take-profit and a stop go in together as an OCO pair.
questions.lesson_line: With a bracket, the stop is in the moment you're filled.

wrong.Trailing stop: A trailing stop is one exit that moves with price. This ticket has an entry and two fixed exits.
wrong.Stop-limit order: A stop-limit is one order with two prices. This is three linked orders.
wrong.Fill-or-kill: Fill-or-kill is a size and timing condition: all of it now, or cancel.

questions.q: What does an OCO order do?
choices: Two orders: one fills, other cancels
One order: all of it or none
One order fills, then triggers a second
Cancels if not filled right away
questions.answer: Two orders: one fills, other cancels
questions.why: Two orders: one fills, the other cancels. Pair a target and a stop as an OCO and the first to fill kills the other.
questions.lesson_line: OCO keeps your two exits from both firing.

questions.q: Tap the order link that fits the blank.
questions.sentence: My target and my stop cover the same 300 shares, linked as an ___ so one fill kills the other.
questions.why: OCO, one-cancels-the-other. When the target fills, the stop is canceled, so it can't sell shares you no longer own.
questions.lesson_line: Two exits on one position: link them as an OCO.

questions.q: How do you set up the two entries?
questions.story: A stock trades at $21. You'll buy a pullback at $20 or a breakout over $22.50, whichever comes first. You want only one position.
choices: OCO of buy limit $20, stop $22.50
Buy limit $20 and buy stop $22.50
A bracket order on the $20 buy limit
One buy stop-limit, $20 to $22.50
questions.why: An OCO with a buy limit at $20 and a buy stop at $22.50. Whichever fills first cancels the other, so you can't end up with both.
questions.lesson_line: Two ways in, one position: link the entries as an OCO.

wrong.Buy limit $20 and buy stop $22.50: Separate orders can both fill. A pop to $22.50 and then a drop to $20 doubles your position.
wrong.A bracket order on the $20 buy limit: A bracket attaches exits to one entry. It doesn't cancel your breakout entry.
wrong.One buy stop-limit, $20 to $22.50: Buy stops must sit above the price, and $20 is below it. One order can't be both entries.

questions.q: On an order ticket, what does the time in force set?
choices: How long the order stays live
The price that triggers it
How many shares can fill
When the trade settles
questions.answer: How long the order stays live
questions.why: How long the order stays live. Day and good 'til canceled are the common time-in-force choices.
questions.lesson_line: Every order has a clock. Check it before you send.

wrong.How many shares can fill: That's the quantity, plus size conditions like all-or-none.
wrong.When the trade settles: Settlement is a separate clock that runs after the trade.

questions.q: If you don't set a time limit, your order is usually a day order.
questions.why: True. Unless you pick a time frame, an order is good only for the trading day you enter it.
questions.lesson_line: No time limit chosen means today only.

questions.q: What happens to your order?
questions.story: At 2 p.m. you place a day order to buy at a $30.00 limit. It doesn't fill by the close. After hours, the stock trades at $29.80.
choices: Nothing, it expired at the close
It fills after hours near $29.80
It waits for tomorrow's open
questions.answer: Nothing, it expired at the close
questions.why: Nothing, it expired at the close. An unfilled day order generally cancels at the end of regular hours. It doesn't carry into after-hours or the next day.
questions.lesson_line: A day order dies at the close. If you still want it, enter it again.

wrong.It fills after hours near $29.80: A day order doesn't carry into the extended-hours session. It was gone at the close.
wrong.It waits for tomorrow's open: That's what a GTC order would do. A day order doesn't carry to the next day.

questions.q: What does good 'til canceled (GTC) mean on an order?
choices: Live until filled or you cancel
Live only for today's session
Fill now or cancel at once
Live for this week only
questions.answer: Live until filled or you cancel
questions.why: Live until it fills or you cancel. A GTC order carries past today, within your broker's time limit.
questions.lesson_line: GTC outlives the day. Keep track of what you've left working.

wrong.Live for this week only: GTC isn't a set week. It runs until it fills or you cancel, within your broker's limit.

questions.q: Good 'til canceled works the same at every broker, with the same time limit.
questions.why: False. How long a GTC order can stay open varies by broker. Check your broker's limit before you count on an old order.
questions.lesson_line: Good 'til canceled isn't forever. Know your broker's limit.

questions.q: You send an immediate-or-cancel (IOC) order to buy 800 shares. Only 300 can fill right away. How many shares get canceled?
questions.why: 500. IOC fills what it can at once and cancels the rest: 800 less 300.
questions.lesson_line: IOC takes what's there now and walks away from the rest.

questions.q: Which instruction fits?
questions.story: You want 5,000 shares. You'll take them only if all 5,000 fill right now. Otherwise, forget it.
choices: Fill-or-kill (FOK)
Immediate-or-cancel (IOC)
All-or-none (AON)
Good 'til canceled (GTC)
questions.why: Fill-or-kill. It must fill right away and in full, or the whole order cancels. No partial fill is allowed.
questions.lesson_line: FOK: all of it, right now, or nothing.

wrong.Immediate-or-cancel (IOC): IOC keeps whatever part fills right away. You could end up with a partial.
wrong.All-or-none (AON): AON wants all of it too, but it can sit and wait. You said now or never.
wrong.Good 'til canceled (GTC): GTC is about how long the order lives. It says nothing about filling all at once.

questions.q: What happens to each?
questions.story: Two orders to buy 1,000 shares. Only 400 are offered at your price right now. Order A is fill-or-kill. Order B is all-or-none.
choices: A cancels; B waits for all 1,000
Both buy 400 and cancel the rest
A buys 400; B cancels
Both wait for all 1,000
questions.answer: A cancels; B waits for all 1,000
questions.why: A cancels, B waits. Fill-or-kill needs everything right now or it's gone. All-or-none also needs everything, but it stays active until it fills or you cancel.
questions.lesson_line: FOK and AON both refuse a partial. Only FOK refuses to wait.

wrong.Both buy 400 and cancel the rest: That's immediate-or-cancel. Neither order here accepts a partial fill.
wrong.A buys 400; B cancels: Backwards. Fill-or-kill never takes a partial, and all-or-none can wait.
wrong.Both wait for all 1,000: Fill-or-kill can't wait. It cancels at once if it can't fill in full.

questions.q: Tap the order that fits the blank.
questions.sentence: I want to buy right at today's closing price, so I'll send a ___ order.
questions.why: Market-on-close. It's meant to fill at the closing price, and any part that misses the closing trade is canceled.
questions.lesson_line: On-close orders trade the closing price, or not at all.

questions.q: On your order screen, what does a fill mean?
choices: An executed order, or its price
An order still waiting to trade
Shares left after a cancel
The total shares traded today
questions.answer: An executed order, or its price
questions.why: An executed order, or the price it executed at. Filled means it traded.
questions.lesson_line: A fill is a done trade. Until then, it's just an order.

wrong.An order still waiting to trade: That's a working order. Nothing has traded yet.
wrong.Shares left after a cancel: Those didn't fill. A fill is what did trade.
wrong.The total shares traded today: That's the day's volume, for everyone. A fill is your own order.

questions.q: One order can fill at more than one price.
questions.why: True. Part of a large order can fill at one price and the rest at others, when one price doesn't hold enough shares.
questions.lesson_line: Big order, thin price: expect several fills and check the average.

questions.q: What is a partial fill?
choices: Only part of your order executed
Your order filled at a worse price
Your broker refused the order
Your order filled after the close
questions.answer: Only part of your order executed
questions.why: Only part of your order executed. The rest is canceled or keeps working, depending on the order's instructions.
questions.lesson_line: Check the filled shares, not just the order. A partial can leave you half in.

wrong.Your order filled at a worse price: That's slippage. An order can fill in full and still fill worse.
wrong.Your broker refused the order: That's a rejected order. Nothing filled.
wrong.Your order filled after the close: That's an after-hours fill. It says nothing about how much filled.

questions.q: Which word names what happened?
questions.story: A trader says after the open: "Only got 300 of my 1,000 before it ran from my limit." Nothing else filled.
choices: Partial fill
Slippage
Rejected order
Fill-or-kill
questions.why: Partial fill. Only part of the order executed at the limit before price moved away. The rest never filled.
questions.lesson_line: A limit protects your price, so on a runner you may get only part.

wrong.Slippage: Slippage is a worse price than expected. Here the price was fine. The size fell short.
wrong.Rejected order: A rejected order fills nothing. This one got 300 shares.
wrong.Fill-or-kill: A fill-or-kill order would have canceled. It never takes part of an order.

questions.q: Where do you stand?
questions.story: Your GTC limit order to buy 2,000 shares has 600 filled. The stock then moved up and away from your limit.
choices: You own 600; 1,400 are still working
The order is done; 1,400 were canceled
You own 2,000 at an average price
Nothing counts until all 2,000 fill
questions.why: You own 600, and 1,400 are still working. A GTC order lasts until it fills in full or is canceled, so the rest waits at your limit.
questions.lesson_line: After a partial, decide: leave the rest working or cancel it. Don't forget it's there.

wrong.The order is done; 1,400 were canceled: That's how a day order ends at the close, or an IOC right away. A GTC keeps working.
wrong.You own 2,000 at an average price: Only 600 traded. You don't own shares that never filled.
wrong.Nothing counts until all 2,000 fill: That's all-or-none. A plain limit order can fill in parts.

questions.q: What is slippage on a trade?
choices: Your fill vs. the price you expected
The gap between the bid and the ask
The day's high minus the day's low
A price gap between two trading days
questions.answer: Your fill vs. the price you expected
questions.why: Your fill vs. the price you expected. It's the difference between the price you planned on and the price you got.
questions.lesson_line: Slippage is the cost of getting filled in a moving market. Plan for it.

wrong.The gap between the bid and the ask: That's the spread. Slippage is the gap between your expected price and your fill.
wrong.The day's high minus the day's low: That's the day's range. It isn't about your order at all.
wrong.A price gap between two trading days: That's a gap on the chart. A gap can cause slippage on a stop, but it isn't slippage.

questions.q: You send a market buy for 1,000 shares with the ask at $15.20. They fill at an average of $15.29. What did slippage cost you?
questions.why: $90. A market buy generally fills at or near the ask, so $15.20 was the price you expected. You paid an average of $15.29 across 1,000 shares.
questions.lesson_line: Size into a thin offer and you pay up. Use a limit when the price matters.

questions.q: Slippage can work in your favor.
questions.why: True. Slippage is any difference from the price you expected, and a fill can come in better. It just isn't promised.
questions.lesson_line: Hope for better fills. Plan for worse ones.

questions.q: Where is slippage on your stop most likely to be worst?
questions.story: You hold four stocks, the same size in each. Each has a sell stop the same distance below its price.
choices: A thinly traded stock on big news
A heavily traded stock on big news
A thinly traded stock on a quiet day
A heavily traded stock on a quiet day
questions.answer: A thinly traded stock on big news
questions.why: A thinly traded stock on big news. Slippage is most common when prices move fast and few buyers and sellers are around.
questions.lesson_line: Thin and fast is where stops fill worst. Expect it there.

wrong.A heavily traded stock on big news: Fast, but deep. Plenty of orders to fill against, so the fill usually lands nearer the stop than in a thin name.
wrong.A thinly traded stock on a quiet day: Thin, but calm. With little movement, price has less room to run past your stop.
wrong.A heavily traded stock on a quiet day: Deep and calm. That's where fills land closest to the stop.

questions.q: What is a short sale?
choices: Selling borrowed shares, rebuy later
Selling shares on the day you buy them
Selling at a loss to cut risk
Selling part of a winning position
questions.why: Selling borrowed shares and buying them back later. You profit if the price falls and lose if it rises.
questions.lesson_line: Short means you sold first. You still owe the shares back.

wrong.Selling shares on the day you buy them: That's a day trade. You owned the shares first.
wrong.Selling at a loss to cut risk: That's taking a loss on shares you own.
wrong.Selling part of a winning position: That's selling partials, trimming shares you own.

questions.q: Before a short sale, the broker must have reasonable grounds the shares can be borrowed. What's that called?
choices: Locate
Margin call
Short interest
Buy to cover
questions.why: Locate. Regulation SHO requires it before the short sale, and it has to be documented.
questions.lesson_line: No locate, no short. That's the rule, not a broker courtesy.

wrong.Margin call: A margin call asks you to add cash or securities when your account falls short.
wrong.Short interest: Short interest is the total of open short positions in a stock.
wrong.Buy to cover: That's the order that closes a short.

questions.q: Your broker can get the locate after your short sale goes through, as long as it's the same day.
questions.why: False. The locate must be made and documented before the short sale, not after.
questions.lesson_line: The locate comes first. Then the short.

questions.q: Tap the word that fits the blank.
questions.sentence: You can't sell what you don't have, so a short seller has to ___ the shares first.
questions.why: Borrow. When you sell short, your broker usually lends you the shares. The loan can carry a fee, from nothing on the most liquid names to a lot on scarce ones.
questions.lesson_line: A short starts with a loan of shares. Check what the borrow costs.

questions.q: Your platform flags a stock as hard to borrow. What does that tell you?
choices: Few shares to lend; fees can be high
Shorting it is banned by federal law
It can't trade until the next open
It's too expensive to buy outright
questions.answer: Few shares to lend; fees can be high
questions.why: Few shares to lend, and fees can be high. Hard-to-borrow stocks are scarce for short sales, and a short order may even be refused.
questions.lesson_line: Hard to borrow means expensive to short, or impossible. Price it in first.

wrong.Shorting it is banned by federal law: It's about the broker's supply of shares, not a law. You may still short it, at a cost.
wrong.It can't trade until the next open: Borrow has nothing to do with trading hours.
wrong.It's too expensive to buy outright: Buying doesn't need a borrow. The flag is about shorting.

questions.q: Which word most likely explains it?
questions.story: You try to short a small, heavily shorted stock. Your broker rejects the order. Yesterday the same order went through.
choices: Hard to borrow
Partial fill
Slippage
Day order
questions.why: Hard to borrow. In heavily shorted names the shares to lend can run out, and then the broker can refuse the short.
questions.lesson_line: On a crowded short, the borrow can vanish from one day to the next. Check it before you plan the trade.

wrong.Partial fill: Nothing filled. The order was refused.
wrong.Slippage: Slippage needs a fill. Yours never traded.
wrong.Day order: A day order is a time limit. It wouldn't block the short.

questions.q: Once you're short, the fee to borrow the shares stays fixed until you cover.
questions.why: False. The cost to borrow can change, sometimes sharply and without warning, as supply and demand for the shares shift.
questions.lesson_line: Check the borrow rate while you hold a short, not just when you enter.

questions.q: You're short 200 shares. Which order action closes the position?
choices: Buy to cover
Sell
Sell short
questions.why: Buy to cover. You close a short by buying the shares back and returning them to the lender.
questions.lesson_line: Sell short to open. Buy to cover to close.

wrong.Sell: Sell is for shares you own. You own none here. You owe 200.
wrong.Sell short: That sells more borrowed shares and makes the short bigger.

questions.q: Tap the word that fits the blank.
questions.sentence: It ran against my short, so I bought the shares back to ___ at a loss.
questions.why: Cover. Buying back shares to close a short is covering. Above your short price, that's a loss.
questions.lesson_line: Covering is the buy that ends a short.

questions.q: You short 200 shares at $18.00. A squeeze hits and you buy to cover at $27.40. How much did you lose, before costs?
questions.why: $1,880. On a short you lose what the price rose: $27.40 less $18.00, on 200 shares.
questions.lesson_line: A short loses as price rises, and price can keep rising. Have your buy stop in.

questions.q: What is a short squeeze?
choices: Short covering lifts the price fast
Sellers dumping shares sink the price
A stock stuck in a tight price range
A broker forcing longs to sell shares
questions.answer: Short covering lifts the price fast
questions.why: Shorts rushing to cover lift the price. A sharp rise pressures short sellers to buy back, and their buying pushes the price up even more.
questions.lesson_line: In a squeeze, the shorts become the buyers.

wrong.Sellers dumping shares sink the price: That's a selloff, the opposite direction.
wrong.A stock stuck in a tight price range: That's a tight range. Nobody is being forced to buy.
wrong.A broker forcing longs to sell shares: That's closer to a margin call. A squeeze is about shorts buying back.

questions.q: Heavy short interest means a short squeeze is coming.
questions.why: False. Heavy short interest means many people think the price will fall. It doesn't mean it will rise, and claims that a squeeze is coming can be false.
questions.lesson_line: Short interest is a crowd, not a catalyst. I'd want a real reason to own it.

questions.q: What's the move?
questions.story: You're short a heavily shorted stock. It gaps up on news and keeps climbing as shorts buy back. It's nearing your buy stop.
choices: Let the buy stop take you out
Cancel the stop and wait it out
Short more at the higher price
Wait for the close to decide
questions.answer: Let the buy stop take you out
questions.why: Let the buy stop take you out. In a squeeze, shorts' buying feeds the rise, and a short's loss has no ceiling. The stop is there for exactly this.
questions.lesson_line: On a short, honor the buy stop. A squeeze can keep running, and the loss has no ceiling.

wrong.Cancel the stop and wait it out: That removes your only exit while the loss has no limit.
wrong.Short more at the higher price: Adding to a short while shorts are being squeezed makes a losing trade bigger.
wrong.Wait for the close to decide: A stop doesn't wait for the close, and neither does a squeeze.

questions.q: What does short interest measure?
choices: Total open short positions in a stock
Shares sold short in a single day
The yearly fee to borrow a stock
Shares the company itself bought back
questions.answer: Total open short positions in a stock
questions.why: Total open short positions in a stock. It's a snapshot on a set date, not today's short selling.
questions.lesson_line: Short interest counts positions still open. Daily short volume is a different number.

wrong.Shares sold short in a single day: That's short sale volume. FINRA says it is not the same as short interest.
wrong.The yearly fee to borrow a stock: That's the borrow fee, usually quoted as a yearly rate.
wrong.Shares the company itself bought back: That's a buyback. It has nothing to do with shorts.

questions.q: Next week XYZ trades down to $47.50. What happens?
questions.story: Your order screen shows: Sell 200 XYZ, type Stop, stop price $47.50, time in force GTC. XYZ closes today at $49.
choices: It turns into a market sell order
Nothing, it expired at today's close
It sells exactly at $47.50 a share
It becomes a limit order at $47.50
questions.answer: It turns into a market sell order
questions.why: It turns into a market order to sell. GTC kept it live past today, and at the stop price a stop becomes a market order. The fill can come in below $47.50.
questions.lesson_line: Read the order type and the time in force together. They decide what happens, and when.

wrong.Nothing, it expired at today's close: That's what a day order would do. This one is GTC.
wrong.It sells exactly at $47.50 a share: The stop price is a trigger, not a promised price.
wrong.It becomes a limit order at $47.50: That's a stop-limit. The type here is a plain stop.

questions.q: What is this order for?
questions.story: Your order screen shows: Buy to cover 100 ABC, type Stop, stop price $31.00. ABC trades at $28.50.
choices: Protecting a short from a rise
Buying a breakout above $31
Covering the short right now
Selling 100 shares at $31
questions.answer: Protecting a short from a rise
questions.why: Protecting a short from a rise. Buy to cover closes a short, and a buy stop above the price only triggers if the stock rises to it.
questions.lesson_line: Buy to cover with a stop above the price: that's a short's protective stop.

wrong.Buying a breakout above $31: A breakout entry would be a plain buy. Buy to cover only closes a short.
wrong.Covering the short right now: It's a stop. It waits, and only buys if ABC rises to $31.
wrong.Selling 100 shares at $31: It's a buy, not a sell.

conflicts: GTC time limits differ by broker and by source: the SEC bulletin says the limit 'may vary based on the brokerage firm'; Fidelity's FAQ says open GTC orders expire after 180 calendar days; Schwab says brokers typically allow no more than 90 days; Investopedia says most brokers use 30 to 90 days. No question keys a number. q30's why and w2 say 'within your broker's time limit', and q31 keys only that the limit varies.

Default order type: FINRA's Order Types page and the SEC's Market Order glossary both say brokers typically enter a market order unless you specify otherwise. Individual platforms' ticket presets were not surveyed, so q02 is keyed on the official wording ('typically') and its why tells the member to check their own ticket.

Slippage has two published definitions. Nasdaq's glossary (Tier 1): the difference between estimated and actual transaction costs, 'usually' from price difference or spread and commission revisions. Investopedia (Tier 2): expected price vs executed price. Every slippage key uses the price sense, which Nasdaq's 'price difference' covers; the commission is never offered as a wrong answer for what slippage is, so neither definition is contradicted.

Bracket naming: Schwab and Interactive Brokers call entry-plus-linked-exits a 'bracket'; Fidelity calls the same structure one-triggers-a-one-cancels-the-other (OTOCO). Questions use 'bracket' and cite Fidelity's OTOCO text as the same structure (q23).

Trailing stop wording: the SEC bulletin defines a trailing stop as 'a stop or stop limit order'; Schwab's advanced-orders article says trailing stops 'are not orders per se' but a way to move stops. The file follows the SEC definition; q17's distractor 'A stop that turns into a limit order' is explained as the stop-limit definition, since what makes a stop trailing is the moving price (a trailing stop-limit exists, per the SEC and thinkorswim pages).

Outdated lines seen and NOT used: Fidelity's FAQ short-sale example says 'Three trading days later, on settlement date' and Nasdaq's 'Execution' glossary says stocks settle in three days (US settlement has been T+1 since May 2024); the SEC Key Points page says the locate is 'usually done two days before settlement' (written for T+2); Investopedia's squeeze page speaks of short positions' 'expiration date' (a stock short has none). No fact or question relies on them.

Stop triggers: the SEC says some firms trigger stops on last-sale prices and others on quotes. q13's story has the stock trade at $44.80 for a few minutes, through a $45 sell stop, so the key holds under either standard; no question asks which standard a broker uses.

Locate sources: the SEC's 'Key Points About Regulation SHO' page (last modified 2022) explains the locate in plain words; the current rule text (eCFR, 17 CFR 242.203(b)(1)) is cited beside it so the rule is checked as it stands today. Both say the same thing: the borrow condition comes before the short sale.

Rejected short (q50): a broker can also refuse a short order for reasons the unit does not teach (for example the Rule 201 short-sale price test, or an account without margin). None of those is a choice, and among the four words offered only hard to borrow can block a short, so the question asks which word 'most likely' explains it.

Slippage judgment (q44): the sources name two drivers, fast markets (FINRA, SEC, Investopedia) and thin liquidity (Investopedia, SEC 'prices of available liquidity'). No source ranks them, so the key is the only choice with both; each wrong choice carries one driver or neither, and its note says which.
